Getting Started with Python Data Analysis

A beginner-friendly walkthrough of pandas, matplotlib, and Jupyter.
Author

Your Name

Published

March 15, 2024

Data analysis is one of the most in-demand skills of the decade, and Python’s ecosystem makes it
remarkably accessible. In this post we’ll cover the essentials: loading data with pandas,
exploring it visually with matplotlib, and running everything interactively in Jupyter.

Setting Up Your Environment

Before writing a single line of analysis code, you need a working environment. The fastest path
is a virtual environment with the three core packages installed.

python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate      # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install pandas matplotlib jupyter
TipPro Tip

Always check for missing values with df.isnull().sum() before any analysis. Silently missing
data is the leading cause of misleading results.

Once installed, launch Jupyter with jupyter notebook and create a new Python 3 kernel.

Loading and Exploring Data

The first thing you’ll do in almost every project is load a CSV file and peek at its shape.

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")
print(df.head())

After df.head() you’ll want a quick statistical summary:

Method What it shows
df.shape (rows, columns)
df.dtypes data type per column
df.describe() count, mean, std, min/max
df.isnull().sum() missing values per column

These four lines form a reliable first-pass audit of any new dataset.

Visualising with Matplotlib

A histogram is the fastest way to understand the distribution of a numeric column.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
ax.hist(df["value_column"], bins=30, color="#3B82F6", edgecolor="white")
ax.set_title("Distribution of value_column")
ax.set_xlabel("Value")
ax.set_ylabel("Frequency")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("distribution.png", dpi=150)
plt.show()

“A picture is worth a thousand words—and in data analysis, a good chart is worth a thousand
rows of summary statistics.”

— Hadley Wickham, R for Data Science

Next Steps

You now have the foundation. From here, the natural progressions are:

  • Seaborn for statistical plots with less boilerplate
  • Plotly for interactive, web-ready visualisations
  • scikit-learn when you’re ready to move from exploration to modelling
  • Polars as a faster alternative to pandas for large datasets

Keep iterating, keep plotting, and don’t be afraid to look at your data from five different
angles before drawing any conclusions.
